column2: (Maitrayani, Kaushitaki, Brihajjabala, Tapani, Kalagnirudra, Maitreyi, Subala, Kshurika, Mantrika — the Upanishads of this group are listed.) Om. There was a king named Brihadratha, who, having established his eldest son in the kingdom, thinking "this body is impermanent," went to the forest in dispassion. There he practised the highest austerity, gazing at the sun with his arms raised. At the end of a thousand days the sage Shakayanya, the venerable knower of the Self, came near, blazing like a smokeless fire, as if burning with his radiance, and said to the king: "Arise, arise! Choose a boon." The king bowed to him and said: "Venerable one, I do not know the Self; you know the truth, and we have heard that you do. Tell us that." (Shakayanya said:) "This is a choice that was made in earlier times and is hard to fulfil; do not ask this question, O descendant of Ikshvaku; choose other desires." Touching Shakayanya's feet, the king spoke this verse:

Venerable one, in this foul-smelling, worthless body — which is a mass of bone, skin, sinew, marrow, flesh, semen, blood, phlegm, tears, excrement, urine, wind, bile and mucus — what is the use of enjoying desires?

In this body, struck by desire, anger, greed, fear, despair, envy, separation from the loved, union with the unloved, hunger, thirst, old age, death, disease and sorrow — what is the use of enjoying desires?
And we see that all this is perishable, like these gnats and mosquitoes, which arise and perish like blades of grass.

And what of these? There are others — great archers, emperors such as Sudyumna, Bhuridyumna, Indradyumna, Kuvalayashva, Yauvanashva, Vadhryashva, Ashvapati, Shashabindu, Harishchandra, Ambarisha, Nanukta, Sharyati, Yayati, Anaranya, Akshasena — and kings like Marutta and Bharata, who, while their kinsfolk looked on, gave up their great glory and went from this world to the next.
And what of these? We also see the restraint of others — of gandharvas, asuras, yakshas, rakshasas, spirits, hosts of ghouls, serpents, planets and the like.

And what of these? We see the drying up of great oceans, the falling of mountain peaks, the shaking of the pole star, the sinking of the earth, and the gods departing from their places. In such a world of rebirth as this, what is the use of enjoying desires, when one who is attached to them is seen returning here again and again? Deign to lift me out. In this world of rebirth I am like a frog in a blind well. Venerable one, you are my refuge — you are my refuge.

Then the venerable Shakayanya, well pleased, said to the king: "Great king Brihadratha, banner and crest of the Ikshvaku line, you have fulfilled your task and are renowned by the name Marut. This Self of yours — which, venerable one, is to be described?" He said to him:

The one who, rising upward by resting on nothing external, dispels darkness — trembling yet untrembling — this, says the venerable one, is the Self. And that serenity which, rising from this body, attains the supreme light and appears in its own form — this is the Self, he said; "this is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman."

Now, O king, this knowledge of Brahman, the knowledge of all the Upanishads, was expounded to us by the venerable Maitreya; I shall tell it to you. It is heard that the Valakhilyas, whose sins were removed, of sharp radiance, with restrained seed, then said to Prajapati: "Venerable one, this body is like a cart, without consciousness. To whom does this greatness belong, of one beyond the senses, by whom it has been made to stand as if conscious? Who is its impeller? Tell us this, venerable one." He said to them:

The one who is heard to stand above speech is this pure, cleansed, empty, tranquil, breath-like, non-ruling self, infinite, imperishable, firm, eternal, unborn, independent, abiding in its own greatness. By him this body has been made to stand as if conscious, and he is its impeller. They said: "Venerable one, how has this body been made to stand as if conscious by one so free from wishes, and how is he its impeller?" He said to them:

That one is subtle, ungraspable, invisible, called the Person; he acts here with intelligence in advance, and by a part of himself awakens the one asleep, with intelligence in advance. That part of his which is mere consciousness, the knower of the field in each person, marked by intention, determination and self-conceit, is Prajapati, called Vishvaksha. By this conscious one this body has been made to stand as if conscious, and he is its impeller. They said: "Venerable one, how does such a one act through a part?" He said to them:

Prajapati stood alone in the beginning; he did not delight, being alone. He meditated on himself and created many creatures. He saw them unaware of themselves, lifeless, standing like posts. He did not delight, and thought: 'To awaken them, I shall enter within.' Making himself like the wind, he entered within. Being one, he could not enter; so he divided himself fivefold, and is called: the up-breath (prana), the down-breath (apana), the equalising breath (samana), the upward breath (udana) and the diffusing breath (vyana).

That which moves upward is the prana; that which moves downward is the apana; that which places the grossest part of food in the apana and carries the finest equally to every limb is the samana; that which brings up and swallows what has been drunk and eaten is the udana; and that which pervades these channels is the vyana.

Then the upamshu and the antaryama overcome each other; between them is the warmth, like the warmth of flesh: that is the Person. That Person is the fire Vaishvanara. It is also said elsewhere: 'This is the fire Vaishvanara, the infinite Person by whom this food that is eaten is cooked.' Its sound is what one hears on covering the ears; when a person is about to depart, he no longer hears this sound.

Having divided himself fivefold, he is hidden in the cave — made of mind, with the body of breath, of many forms, of true will: the Self. Dwelling within the heart, unfulfilled, he thought, 'Let me enjoy objects.' Having broken through the openings, he rose up with five rays and enjoys the objects. The senses of knowledge are his rays; the senses of action are his horses; the body is the chariot; the mind is the charioteer; the whip is made of Nature. Urged by it, this body revolves like a wheel. Without him this body, made to stand as if conscious, would not be — and he is its impeller.

That Self, as if brought under the sway of bright and dark fruits of action, as if overcome by them, moves in each body; because of being unmanifest, subtle, invisible, ungraspable and free from the sense of 'mine', it is unsteady — a non-doer that stays as though a doer.

That Self is pure, steady, unmoving, untouched, unhurried, free from longing, remaining like a spectator — enjoying the play of its own nature, and staying hidden within a veil woven of the qualities — it stays, it stays.

They said: "Venerable one, if you thus point out the greatness of this Self, then who is that other, superior one — the self overcome by bright and dark fruits of action, attaining a good or bad birth, going downward or upward, wandering overcome by the pairs of opposites? Who is he?" He said to them:

There is indeed another, lower, the elemental self, which, overcome by bright and dark fruits of action, enters a good or bad womb, and wanders in a downward or upward course, overcome by the pairs. Its explanation is this: the five subtle elements are called by the word 'elements'; the five gross elements are also called by the word 'elements'; and the aggregate of these is called the body. What is called the body is called the elemental self. Its Self is like a drop on a lotus leaf. Overcome by the qualities of nature, it falls into confusion; being confused, it does not see the Lord who abides in the self, the Impeller; carried along by the floods of the qualities, defiled, unsteady, fickle, greedy, longing and distracted, it falls into conceit, thinking, 'I am he; this is mine' — and so binds the self by the self, like a bird in a net, and wanders overcome by the fruits of what it has done.

It is said elsewhere: 'The doer is this elemental self; the inner Person makes it act through the organs. As an iron ball overcome by fire is struck by smiths and takes on many shapes, so this elemental self, overcome by the inner Person, struck by the qualities, takes on multiplicity. And that which is threefold in quality, transformed into eighty-four hundred thousand wombs — that elemental threefold nature is the form of multiplicity. These qualities are set in motion by the Person as a wheel by its maker. As the fire is not overcome when the iron ball is struck, so the Person is not overcome; it is the elemental self that is overcome, because of its close attachment.'

It is said elsewhere: 'This body arises from sexual union, without awareness; it is a hell itself, passing out by the urinary passage; it is built up of bones, smeared with flesh, bound with skin, filled with faeces, urine, bile, phlegm, marrow, fat, grease and many other impurities — it sits like a treasury.'

It is said elsewhere: 'Delusion, fear, despair, sleep, drowsiness, sores, old age, sorrow, hunger, thirst, meanness, anger, unbelief, ignorance, envy, cruelty, stupidity, shamelessness, dishonesty, violence, inequality — these are the marks of tamas. Craving, affection, passion, greed, harm, sensuality, restlessness, jealousy, fixed desire, fickleness, the wish to snatch, gaining wealth, favouring friends, dependence on possessions, aversion to unwanted sense-objects and attachment to wanted ones — these are the marks of rajas.' Filled with these and overcome by them, this elemental self therefore takes many forms — takes many forms.

Then those sages of restrained seed, very astonished, came together and said: "Venerable one, homage to you! Instruct us; you are our refuge; there is no other. Who is the guest of this elemental self, by whom, leaving this, it attains union with the other?" He said to them:

It is said elsewhere: 'Like waves in great rivers, what has been done before cannot be turned back for him; the coming of his death is as unstoppable as the sea's tide. Like an animal he is bound by ropes made of good and bad results; like a prisoner he has no independence; like one in Yama's realm he is in a state of much fear; like one maddened by liquor, he is intoxicated with a delight that is not real intoxication; he wanders as if seized by an evil spirit, as if bitten by a great serpent; blinded by passion as if in great darkness; like a magic show, made of illusion; like a dream, false vision; like the inside of a plantain stem, without substance; like an actor, a costume for a moment; like a painted wall, falsely charming.' And it is also said: 'The objects such as sound and touch stand as if they were misfortunes. Attached to them, the elemental self does not remember the highest state.'

This is the remedy for this elemental self — namely, the pursuit of knowledge, the practice of duty, and going through the stages of life; in one's own duty everything is held, like a post that supports other branches; by it one rises upward, otherwise one falls down. He who does not, in the Vedas, transgress his own duty, is overcome by his own duty and becomes one who belongs to a stage of life; one who stays in the stages of life is called an ascetic. It is also said: 'Without austerity there is no attainment in meditation on the Self, nor purification of works.' Thus it says: 'By austerity goodness (sattva) is attained; from goodness the mind is attained; by the mind the Self is attained; and by attaining the Self one does not return.'
On this there are these verses: "As a fire without fuel becomes quiet in its own source, so the mind, with its activities ceased, becomes quiet in its own source."
For the mind that has become quiet in its own source, going toward truth, not deluded by sense-objects, the falsehoods that follow from action come to nothing.
The mind alone is the cycle of birth and death; let one purify it with effort. What one's mind is, that one becomes — this is the eternal secret.
By the serenity of the mind one destroys good and bad action. With a serene self, abiding in the Self, one enjoys imperishable happiness.
When a creature's mind is attached to the field of sense-objects — if it were so attached to Brahman, who would not be freed from bondage?
The mind is said to be of two kinds: pure and impure. The impure is that with desire and intention; the pure is that without desire.
Having made the mind free of dullness and distraction, perfectly still — when it reaches the state of no-mind, that is the highest state.
It should be restrained in the heart until it has come to its end. This is knowledge, and this is liberation; the rest is an expansion of books.
The happiness that the mind, whose impurity has been washed away by absorption and which is settled in the Self, obtains — cannot be described in words; it is then grasped by the inner organ itself.
As water in water, fire in fire, space in space is not distinguished, so the person whose mind has gone within is set free.
The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings: attached to sense-objects, it is for bondage; free from objects, it is said to be for liberation.
Now this is the praise by Kutsayana: "You are Brahma, you are Vishnu, you are Rudra, you are Prajapati; you are Agni, Varuna, Vayu; you are Indra, you are the Moon."
You are Manu, you are Yama, you are the Earth, and you are the Unfallen. Both in your own purposes and in your natural aims you abide in heaven in many ways.

Lord of the universe, homage to you! You are the Self of the universe, the maker of the universe's works; the enjoyer of the universe, the illusion of the universe; you delight in the play of the universe, the Lord.
Homage to you of tranquil self; homage to you, the most secret; to the inconceivable, the immeasurable, without beginning or end. Thus.

This was indeed darkness alone; that, impelled by the Supreme, attained differentiation. That is the form of rajas; that rajas, impelled, attained unevenness. That is the form of tamas; that tamas, impelled, flowed forth from itself. That is the form of sattva; that sattva, impelled, flowed forth. From it came that part which is mere consciousness, the knower of the field in each person, marked by intention, determination and self-conceit — Prajapati. His principal bodies have been declared: Brahma, Rudra, Vishnu. Now, that part of him which is of rajas is this Brahma; that part of him which is of tamas is this Rudra; and that part of him which is of sattva is Vishnu. So this One becomes threefold, and appears eightfold, elevenfold, twelvefold and immeasurably; because of his manifestation he moves among beings, and became the support and lord of all beings. This Self is within and without — within and without.
